Everything in these accounts follows an exceptionally rigorous pattern. As in Swedenborg's Memorabilia, the correspondence is never forgotten between the images seen in the Malakūt—the real imaginal forms, the imaginalia or apparentiae reales—and what is taking place, even in this very world, within the hidden depths of human consciousness. We may say that the “Tale of the White Cloud” is an account of initiation whose purpose, episodes, and consequences are comparable to those of the anagōgē, the spiritual ascent that took on the meaning of a “sacrament of immortality” for the mystical community whose sacred book was probably the Chaldaean Oracles. These Oracles were studied and interpreted with particular devotion by the later Neoplatonists, including Proclus and Syrianus (see above, Book II, Chapter II). For whoever has entered the Malakūt and there reached the Source of Life has been reborn, and is henceforth beyond the reach of death and nothingness.

Qāzī Saʿīd wrote a commentary on this tale so extensive that it constitutes a book in itself; here we can give only its substance. The commentary forms the eleventh and final treatise of his unfinished Summa (see above, p. 131), which was intended to comprise forty treatises (Kitāb al-Arbaʿīniyyāt). The hadith itself does not appear to be recorded in Majlisī's great encyclopedia. Qāzī Saʿīd, however, cites as his authoritative source a collection by Shaykh Ṣadūq Ibn Bābūya, along with two other collections.

We should make clear at once that this account must not be confused with another lengthy narrative, which does appear in Majlisī's encyclopedia and is known as the “Tale of the Carpet” (ḥadīth al-bisāṭ). That narrative describes the journey of the Imam and his companions to visit the Seven Sleepers (see Quran, Sura XVIII), whereas our tale describes a visionary exploration of Mount Qāf, the cosmic and psycho-cosmic mountain.

The “Tale of the White Cloud” is narrated by Salmān Pārsī, also known as Salmān Pāk—Salmān the Persian, or Salmān the Pure. He is a Persian knight of Zoroastrian origin who set out in search of the True Prophet and mysteriously became something like the Prophet of Islam's companion in initiation.

Six individuals are gathered around the First Imam in his house in Medina. Among them are his two young sons, al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, who will later become the Second and Third Imams. The young al-Ḥasan introduces the central theme when he addresses his father with these words: “Solomon, the son of David, asked God for a power such as no one after him would possess [an allusion to Quran 38:35]. Do you possess something of Solomon's power?”

Toward the end of the tale, we shall learn that the Imam, in his metaphysical reality, is the inward essence of every prophetic gift. From the beginning and for all eternity, he is the one who holds the power of the Seal that he himself bestowed upon Solomon. The Imam's affirmative answer to his son's question therefore leads the young al-Ḥasan to express this wish: “We would like to contemplate something of that Malakūt over which God has granted you sovereignty, so that people's faith may grow as our own faith grows” (§§1–3).

The Imam grants this devout wish immediately, and a mysterious journey without movement begins. It will lead our pilgrims first into the Malakūt of the vegetable kingdom, and then into the Malakūt of the realm of organic life. From there they penetrate the Malakūt of human reality, passing through a series of levels: first, the Malakūt of vegetable life within the human being (anima vegetabilis); next, that of organic life within the human being (anima vitalis); and finally, that of the thinking soul (anima rationalis).

This entry into the human Malakūt will be experienced as an ascent to the summit of Mount Qāf, the psycho-cosmic mountain. Since the laws of chronological time have now been suspended, our pilgrims will find themselves living alongside people and events belonging to the “past.” They will then glimpse the secrets of mysterious and distant universes. The entire journey will unfold in five stages.

When the companions return to awareness of this world, they will have become men of the Malakūt. At the end of his commentary, Qāzī Saʿīd will therefore be able to tell his reader: “We have explained all this to you so that you too may take your place with the Imam's companions upon the malakūtī cloud [the White Cloud], and rise with them to the Malakūt.”

The first of these explanations, however—the one prompted by the Imam's gesture that causes the Cloud to appear, and on which our understanding of everything that follows depends—concerns the folding inward of chronological time and the space of the sensible world.
4. The Folding Inward of Chronological Time and Sensible Space

Indeed, the guiding thread of Qāzī Saʿīd's commentary, from one episode to the next, is the initiates' entry, under the Imam's guidance, first into the Malakūt of space and then into the Malakūt of time. This entry, by its very nature, causes the space and time of the sensible world to fold inward.

Admittedly, from this point of view, space occupies a privileged position in relation to time. At the level of physics, Qāzī Saʿīd explains, we must approach the question of space through the surfaces of physical objects. At the metaphysical level, however, what concerns us is the Space of spaces, understood as the Throne (ʿarsh) of everything that has spatial existence. Even the word “distance,” when used at this level, can be understood only by analogy with our own world. Everything in this world is like an outer husk enclosing the kernel that is the other world; physical surface is itself no more than the husk surrounding the distance with which metaphysics is concerned.

Yet at whatever level we consider it, space belongs to the order of what is simultaneous and stable, whereas time, at the physical level, belongs essentially to the order of what is successive and unstable. When this time folds back into a higher order of time, its instability comes to an end: the temporal order is stabilized into a spatial order. Here we may recall Gurnemanz's words to Parsifal: “Here, my son, time becomes space.”

The drama unfolded by the account of initiation thus appears as a redemption of time, a reclaiming of what has been surrendered to time, precisely insofar as the initiate is admitted into the space of the Malakūt. This is one of the most important perspectives from which we must contemplate the hadith of the White Cloud and its commentary.

We must therefore keep in mind the philosophy of time that preoccupied our author throughout so many pages of his works, and that ultimately provides the key to his commentary on the “Tale of the White Cloud.” He deals with it explicitly in the prologue and returns to it once more during the final episode.

Indeed, as soon as we confront the questions raised by hermeneutics—by the spiritual understanding of the Quran's true meaning—we cannot avoid appealing to an interpretation of time itself, to the philosophy of the “forms of temporality” developed by Qāzī Saʿīd Qummī (see above, Book I, Chapter III, section 5).

We are well aware that a full account of this theme, as treated by our philosophers, would require an entire book. Nevertheless, we cannot proceed without drawing from Qāzī Saʿīd's commentary on the “Tale of the White Cloud” a few fundamental observations that complement the more extended analyses he has offered elsewhere.

First, Qāzī Saʿīd firmly rejects the notion of time as a line stretching from pre-eternity (azal) to post-eternity (abad). If he must give time a geometrical form, he prefers that of a sphere or circle representing the “time of times,” or “absolute time.” The capacity of this sphere or circle corresponds exactly to that of the sphere or circle representing the “Space of spaces,” or absolute space. The two spheres are coextensive: they coincide in their entirety and already coexist as complete wholes.

Unfortunately, this is not how time appears “among us”—what our author calls dense, compact time, the time of the sensible world. Because the perceiving subject is confined within the narrow limits of sense organs belonging to a material body of an inferior order, the different parts of time, space, and movement do not coexist for that subject. Their coexistence cannot be perceived.

As Qāzī Saʿīd writes: “The one who is chained within the Sijjīn [the abyss, hell] of sensible perceptions is incapable of perceiving all the parts of time and movement simultaneously. But the inability to perceive something does not mean that what is not perceived does not exist. Nothing prevents these parts from coexisting within the vessel of everlasting duration (fī ẓarf al-dahr, the Aeon), and from being present there simultaneously.”

Everything changes, of course, when the perishable body of material flesh is replaced by a subtle body whose very substance is pure light (mādda nūriyya). Such are the bodies of the Imams. They were created from the purest portion of the substance from which the spirits of creatures were formed: the subtle body of light belonging to the Throne (jism laṭīf nūrī ʿarshī). The original body of their followers, too, was created from the radiance of the Imams' light.

“Movement, with all its pasts and futures, and time, with all its pre-eternities and post-eternities, as they appear to anyone observing sensible things, are two magnitudes that rise upon the carpet of stability and permanence. Both are oriented toward the Kaaba of the All-Powerful King. They carry the actions of human beings from the abode of transience to the abode of enduring existence.

“Thus the days and nights are like a line of camels bringing the caravan of creatures toward the abode of stability, while the months and years that have passed move to meet the ‘Promised Day,’ accompanied by the clouds of evening and the clouds of morning.

“But consider the mountains. Although they appear fixed to our senses and our ordinary powers of judgment, they are perpetually moving—as the Quranic verse says: ‘You see the mountains and think them motionless, yet they move as the clouds move’ (27:90). In the same way, but in the opposite direction, times and moments, despite their passing and coming to an end, are stable essences, permanent realities, when seen by the Intelligence and the Soul of the World.

“The modes of existence that prevail among sensible things are therefore reversed. The knower must understand that apparent [outward] fixity does not exclude hidden [inward] movement, and that restlessness [movement] at the sensible level does not exclude repose, stability, and permanence at the level of the Intelligence [Nous]…

“Space and time, to the gaze that penetrates to the depths of things, are two corresponding planes or levels, two sublime Thrones for the beings above and the beings below. In their union and stability, pre-eternity and post-eternity embrace one another within a single moment; manifestation and concealment embrace one another within a single place. When they separate and appear gradually, the first becomes distinct from the last, and the hidden [the inward] becomes distinct from the manifest [the outward].”

To understand this, Qāzī Saʿīd explains, we must imagine that everything which concretely exists—whether in a material state, that is, compact and dense, or in a spiritual state, that is, subtle—forms a unity, a single individuality. Just as each individual being has its own quantity (miqdār) of matter and its own measure of space, so each has its own measure of time: a unique, personal time, possessing dimensions of length and breadth. Every individuality thus has a time different from every other individuality's time, just as it occupies a place different from the place occupied by another. Contemporaneity in the true sense therefore presupposes at least some correspondence between these different times.

Now, something can happen to any given measure of time that resembles what happens to a piece of wax when we compress it or stretch it out. Its shape and extension change, but the quantity of its substance neither increases nor decreases. And so it is with the body and its time: the subtler the body, the subtler its measure of time becomes, and the greater the capacity and extent that time can attain.

There is, then, the compact, dense, opaque time (zamān kathīf) of the sensible world. There is the subtle time (zamān laṭīf) of the “imaginal” world of the Malakūt, which must not be confused with “imaginary time” (zamān mawhūm). Finally, there is the absolutely subtle time (zamān alṭaf) of the intelligible and intellectual world of the Jabarūt.

When speaking of subtle time, we can describe either a folding inward or an expansion of time. It depends on whether we regard the moments dispersed throughout succession as gathered together and made present to the subject, or regard the subject as becoming present to all those moments at once. These are merely two perspectives on one and the same event.

Without any change in its own measure, the time allotted to a spiritual individuality can thus encompass an immense expanse of being. Conversely, that individuality can have before it a multitude—or even the totality—of the moments of existence, all present in perfect synchrony. Succession becomes simultaneity. Time becomes space as it is raised, through successive degrees of refinement, to an ever subtler state of being.

“So long as you have not emerged from the narrow confines of your senses and entered the kingdom of your own Malakūt [that is, the suprasensible realm of your subtle body, as you exist in the celestial world of the Malakūt], you must know—or rather, you must remember—that movement, time, and space correspond to one another at their respective levels [the levels of the Mulk, the Malakūt, and the Jabarūt]. Likewise, the different universes have boundaries and points of reference that correspond to one another.
“The subtler space becomes, as we pass through these universes arranged in ascending degrees of subtlety, all the way to absolute subtlety, the subtler movement and time become as well.

“The malakūtī body [the subtle body of light belonging to the Malakūt] possesses perfect subtlety and luminosity. No curtain or barrier can hide anything from it; neither earth nor heaven can obstruct its passage. Such is the condition of the Angels who descend from the supreme station (min al-maqām al-aʿlā) to communicate revelation to the prophets. Such, too, is the condition of the prophets when they rise to the station described in the Quranic verse as ‘the distance of two bows, or nearer still’ (53:9).

“The celestial individualities of the Malakūt (ashkhāṣ malakūtiyya) are not subject to the necessity of being in one particular place rather than another within sensible space. Every place stands in an equal relationship to them. The totality of places, in relation to these beings, is comparable to the relationship of the Earth to Heaven.

“And what is true of space is true also of malakūtī time and malakūtī movement. Their subtlety is such that all the times and movements belonging to our world are gathered and folded into the time and movement of the Malakūt. Indeed, a single portion of malakūtī time or movement, when unfolded, is equivalent to months and years of our own time.
“If this is true of the Malakūt, imagine what must be true of the worlds that stand even higher than it.”

Qāzī Saʿīd recalls this entire theory of subtle time and space at the beginning of his commentary because the whole interpretation of the “Tale of the White Cloud” depends upon it. There are two reasons for this.

First, the tale as a whole describes an experience of absolute time, of the simultaneity of different times as they exist permanently within the Malakūt. Second, the experience takes place through the subtle body. Consequently, the measure of time allotted to each participant in the events of the tale undergoes a transformation analogous to what happens to the piece of wax in our philosopher's earlier comparison.

What we find here, then, is a conception of the gradual refinement of “subtle matter” that can be compared—just as Mullā Ṣadrā Shīrāzī has already led us to do elsewhere—with the spissitudo spiritualis, the spiritual density, of the Cambridge Platonists, particularly Henry More. This conception has the power to overcome the dualism of thought and extension that has caused so much difficulty for philosophers in the West.

We can begin to sense all this from the very opening of the tale. The six companions—sons or disciples of the First Imam, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—are gathered in his house, engaged in a spiritual conversation with him. His young son al-Ḥasan addresses to his father the request we read earlier.
In response, the Imam rises, performs a prayer of two rakʿāt—two cycles of ritual prayer—and walks into the courtyard of his house. The disciples keep their eyes fixed upon him.

“Then the Imam stretched out his noble hand toward the west, and held it there until a cloud became visible to us, emerging from the palm of his hand. He spread out this cloud until he caused it to remain suspended above the house. Behind this cloud there was another cloud” (§5).

From the very beginning of this scene, baṣīra, inner vision, is already at work. It is the faculty through which entry into the Malakūt becomes possible. Without realizing it, the participants have been withdrawn from the world of empirical perception. What they are now perceiving is no longer the sensible world.
Every detail marks a stage in this transition. This is why Qāzī Saʿīd attaches such importance to the meaning of each one. Unfortunately, we can retain only what is essential to his interpretation.

Our commentator begins by observing that the secret (sirr) of the scene, from this very moment, is that everything is taking place within the Malakūt. The Imam acts and reveals himself to his companions through his subtle, malakūtī body. But the companions do not yet know this. They will understand only after the scene of “transfiguration” that occurs a little later, when they have all taken their places together upon the White Cloud.

First comes the gesture of the Imam's hand. This hand is in fact a member of the Imam's subtle body, his malakūtī hand (al-yad al-malakūtī). For this hand, there is neither nearness nor distance. Our Earth, compared with the Earth of the Malakūt, which is its inner, hidden reality, is no more than “a walnut in relation to you when you hold it in the hollow of your hand.”
And why does the Imam extend the hand of his subtle, malakūtī body toward the west?

“Because the dimension of walāyat, which is the inward reality and secret of prophecy, is situated on the western side of the higher world, just as the sun of prophecy is situated in the east of that higher world. This is because the Friends of God (Awliyāʾ Allāh) are illuminated by the light of the prophets and are brought to their perfection through the guidance of the prophets.”

The placing of walāyat in the west corresponds to a theme found in other authors, including Shams al-Dīn Lāhījī. In their writings, the cycle of walāyat appears as the night of inward meaning, while the spiritual journey is portrayed as a passage through that night, advancing by way of symbols.

Since the power and sovereignty of the Imams belong to the western side of the higher world—the “place” of walāyat—we can now understand the full meaning of the Imam's gesture at the beginning of the tale, when he stretches the hand of his subtle body toward the west.
As for the two clouds brought into appearance by that gesture, Qāzī Saʿīd suggests their meaning by referring to a hadith of the Sixth Imam, Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq. This tradition states:

“The Imam ʿAlī is sovereign over what is upon the Earth and over what is beneath the Earth. It happened that two clouds appeared before him: a heavy cloud and a light cloud. The Imam chose the heavy cloud. Now, the heavy cloud contained dominion over what is beneath the Earth, while the light cloud contained dominion over what is upon the Earth. But the Imam gave his preference to the heavy cloud.”

Our commentator explains that “what is upon the Earth” means what is apparent, external, and outward—the exoteric. “What is beneath the Earth” means what is hidden, internal, and inward—the esoteric. It does not mean the underworld or hell (infernum) at all, but the Malakūt.

In the hadith we are examining, the light cloud follows the heavy cloud. This is because the Imam commands both. Although he has expressed a preference for the heavy cloud, he remains sovereign over everything upon the Earth and everything beneath it, as the tradition explicitly declares.

Having established this general principle, Qāzī Saʿīd sets out to explain the metaphysical reality (ḥaqīqat) represented by the two clouds. He begins with two premises, from which the truth of what is symbolized will emerge—that is, the truth of the reality perceived imaginally in the form of a “cloud.”

A) The premises. The first is this: the heavy cloud—the first cloud that the Imam's hand “spreads out” in our tale—represents dominion over what lies beneath the Earth, in other words, over inward reality. As such, it gathers time into itself, causing it to fold inward. For the journey through metaphysical realities (ḥaqāʾiq), those belonging to the inward level of existence, takes place outside the laws of chronological time, the dark and dense time called kathīf.

The light cloud, on the other hand—the second cloud in our tale—represents dominion over what is upon the Earth, in other words, over outward reality. It gathers into itself the visible aspect of the Earth: place, and the spatial character of place.

It follows naturally that within the hierarchy of being, this second cloud, representing outward reality, appears only in second position. For the folding inward of time brings about the folding inward of space, and not the other way around.

The second premise is this. The philosophers of divine wisdom hold that every species in the visible world has a corresponding being in the Malakūt. With God's permission, this being governs and protects the species, preserving its unity and holding its multiplicity together.

The Ishrāqiyyūn—the philosophers of illumination belonging to Suhrawardī's Eastern school—call this being the rabb al-nawʿ, the “Lord” or “Angel of the Species.” The work known as the Theology of Aristotle calls it the Kalima, the Logos, or the Word. The philosopher-theologians sometimes speak of a particular divine Name and sometimes of the Angel acting under the authority of that Name.

This malakūtī lord, or Angel of the earthly species, has two faces. Through one face it receives the influence flowing down from what is above it; through the other, it transmits that influence to what is below it.

When the spiritual knower fixes his gaze upon this celestial or malakūtī sovereign, holding his inner vision steadily upon it, he may himself come to be invested with the same quality: that of an intermediary and mediator between two worlds.

B) Having established these premises, Qâzî Sa'îd considers the following. The first cloud, which the Imam stretches out above his dwelling with his hand (the heavy cloud), represents the power of the celestial Angel or lord (malakûtî) over the inner reality of the species he governs—that is, over its malakût, its spiritual or heavenly state. He can therefore enfold time.

The second cloud (the light cloud) represents his power over the outward reality, the molk, or perceptible manifestation, of that species: the power to enfold space. The Imam, however, by virtue of his imamate and his all-embracing walâyat, has authority over both powers, that of the malakût and that of the molk. His case differs, then, from that of Alexander.

For Alexander, only space was enfolded (represented here by the second cloud) when he reached the land of darkness, where Khezr gave him to drink from the Spring of Life. For and through the Imam, both space and time can be enfolded. That double transformation is precisely what drives the action of the “Tale of the White Cloud.”

Qâzî Sa'îd now defines his terms. (a) One being of the Malakût is lord of the Earth's outward reality. He calls this being the Angel or Word of the earthly aspect of Earth (Kalimat arzîya). (b) Another being of the Malakût is lord of the Earth's inner reality. He calls this being the Angel or Word of the Earth's malakût (Kalimat malakûtîya). (c) Above both stands the lord of the Earth's jabarût and lâhût—the Earth at the level of the cherubic Intelligences and at the level of the divine Names. He calls this being the Logos or divine Word (Kalimat ilâhîya).

The metaphysical reality of time lies under the authority of the Angel of the Earth's malakût, its inner reality; it is through this Angel that the time of our chronology is enfolded. That is the meaning of the Imam's gesture when he extends the hand of his “malakûtî body” toward the west of the Malakût, where his walâyat holds sway.

By stretching the “heavy cloud” over his dwelling, he places that earthly dwelling under the authority of the Angel of the Earth's inner reality, who has the power to enfold time. This power acts upon time's original metaphysical reality (haqîqat aslîya), which embraces every past and every future.

When, in a secondary gesture, the Imam extends the second, lighter cloud over his earthly home, he places it under the authority of the Angel of the Earth's outward reality, the Angel who governs earthly space. At the Imam's invitation, the companions then take their places on the first cloud, the White Cloud (ghamâma). This tells us that the Imam has already granted their wish to “enter the Malakût”: he has brought about the enfolding of time and space.

Consequently, measured by the dense time (kathîf) of our ordinary experience, only a very brief interval will be needed for the Imam and his companions to travel to the many worlds mentioned later in the tale. They will see prophets of the past: Sâlih, for example, who was sent to the people of Thamûd. They will see the Imam fight the people of 'Âd, whom the Quran (7:63; 11:52) describes as rejecting the prophet Hôd sent to them. This is possible only because the companions are present (hozûr) in the time inhabited by the people of 'Âd—or, more precisely, present to the time that exists within the people of 'Âd.
“Observe carefully for yourself what you are about to see,” Qâzî Sa'îd tells his reader, “so that your foot does not stumble after it has been made firm”.

Next, the Imam commands a particular breath of wind. Our commentator explains that this breath is the malakût of movement, its Angel: the Logos or divine Word who has authority over the other two Angels, representing respectively the malakût of time and that of space.

The Prophet said of this “celestial” (malakûtî) breeze—the inner reality of the wind our senses perceive in this world—that “it proceeds from the Breath of the Merciful” (Nafas al-Rahmân). Through the faithful service of these three Angels or divine Words, governing movement, time and space, the Imam and his companions will undertake their strange journey over immense distances.
Yet by the “dark and dense” time measured on our clocks, they will have been “absent” from this world for only a few hours.

Salmân the Pure continues his account in the following words. We should now be able to understand the allusions: “Then the Imam made a sign to a certain breath of wind, saying: ‘Come down to us, O wind!’ And I swear by the exalted God: we saw the wind and the cloud descend, saying: ‘We bear witness that there is no god but the One, who has no partner. We bear witness that Mohammad is His servant and Messenger, and that you [the Imam] are the Friend [or One Close to] God.

“Whoever doubts you is already lost. Whoever holds fast to you is already on the path of salvation.’ (We shall encounter this threefold profession of faith, constitutive of Shiite belief, in one episode after another.) Then the two clouds came down until they resembled two carpets, fragrant as musk. The Imam said to us: ‘Take your places on the White Cloud.’ We sat down upon it. Then the Imam said: ‘O wind, carry us away!’ And we were lifted into the heights” (§§ 6–7).

The companions are now present in the Malakût, and their journey is a visionary experience. They perceive the beings and things of its subtle world through the faculties of their own subtle, malakûtî bodies. Naturally, the Imam no longer appears to them clothed in the perishable flesh he assumed during his fleeting earthly manifestation: the form of his earthly humanity (nâsût). They see him as he is in his celestial, divine reality, his “person of theophanic Light,” the light belonging to the fullness, or pleroma, of the eternal Prophetic Reality (Haqîqat mohammadîya).

As they take their places on the White Cloud, the Imam is transfigured before them (metamorphosis). He appears in all the splendour of what Gnostic or Docetist Christology had already called caro spiritualis, spiritual flesh. Qâzî Sa'îd will examine in depth every symbolic detail of this transfiguration.

“Then,” Salmân the Pure's account continues, “upon that cloud we suddenly saw the Imam seated on a Throne of light. He wore two yellow robes. On his head was a diadem of yellow hyacinth; the straps of his sandals sparkled at his feet; and on his finger was a seal of white hyacinth. The light of his Face almost blinded us” (§ 8).

Qâzî Sa'îd explains: the Imam has now cast aside the garment of his earthly humanity (nâsût). He appears to his companions clothed instead in the robe of his sovereignty over the spiritual world of the Malakût. This is the sovereignty of his universal walâyat: his investiture as God's Friend, or One Close to God, in relation to all humanity.

The Imam's Throne represents that sovereignty over the Malakût (over the cloud that is the malakût of time). The Throne therefore belongs to a world higher than the Malakût: the Jabarût, world of the Intelligences, and the Lâhût, world of the divine Names. It is pure, unmixed Light. We still have to explain the symbolism of the transfigured Imam's clothing and adornments in his “celestial” state. That explanation will follow from a theory of colours and their distribution across the three worlds.

The Light flowing from the supreme Principle—the sun in the heaven of the spiritual universes—takes on different colours according to its nearness to or distance from that Source, and therefore according to how pure it remains or how far it is mixed with “material matter” (mâddat jismânîya). Closest to the Orient of lights (mashriq al-Anwâr), the light is white. At the opposite extreme is the blackness of dark bodies, the farthest west, the “last of all wests” (montahâ al-maghârib) to which this light can descend: the point farthest from the Source.

Halfway between white and black is red. (We meet this same theory of colours in Sohrawardî, especially in the “Tale of the Crimson Archangel.”) Between white and red, nearer to the Light of lights, is yellow. Between red and black, nearer the material world, is green. This theory invites comparison both with the ordering of colours derived from the symbolism of the four pillars of the Throne ('arsh) and with the subtle centres (latîfa) of Semnânî's mystical physiology, discussed above (Book IV, chapter iv).

Applying his theory of colours to the three worlds—the highest, comprising the Lâhût and Jabarût; the intermediate world of the Malakût; and the lower world of nâsût, earthly human reality—our philosopher explains that white is the colour of the Lâhût and Jabarût, while black is the colour of nâsût. Between them lies the immense Malakût, containing every intermediate colour between white and black. Whatever lies near the outer boundary of the Malakût, where it adjoins the higher world, is yellow. Red lies midway between the two extremes; as one descends through the Malakût toward nâsût, the colours gradually approach black.

The meaning of the Imam's clothing upon his Throne of light now becomes clear. It follows a single principle: the hierarchy of levels of being. Everything that exists in our world has its source or archetype (asl)—its imaginal metaphysical reality—in the Malakût. Everything in the Malakût, in turn, has its source or archetype in worlds higher still, the Jabarût and Lâhût. Qâzî Sa'îd is, in effect, setting out the rules of an imamological iconography, a way of representing the “Imam in majesty.” The colours correspond to the different levels of the Imam's malakûtî form.

The diadem upon the Imam's head is made of yellow hyacinth. Among the three kingdoms of our world, the mineral kingdom is named first; so it is with the mineral world of the Malakût. The diadem is yellow because it lies close to the higher world, resting as it does upon the Imam's head.

The two robes of the Imam are yellow. Our commentator suggests that they should probably be imagined as a deep yellow, tending toward orange and therefore closer to red, since the torso covered by the robe is nearer than the head to the middle region symbolized by red. The Imam wears two robes, an outer and an inner, perhaps because, having removed the robe of nâsût (the appearance of his earthly humanity), he reveals himself clothed in the double light of the Lâhût and the Malakût.

The sandals. In the Imam's figure, his two feet are the part closest to the material world. They “rest upon this world,” in the sense that his authority extends over it. The hadith does not specify the colour of the sandals or their straps. Qâzî Sa'îd, perhaps remembering the iconographic details of the Prophet's celebrated vision—“I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms”—imagines the sandals as emerald-green and their straps as red hyacinth. The very idea of hyacinth undoubtedly evokes red. But there is more to it. The straps hold the sandals in place, just as the Malakût (spiritual reality) sustains nâsût (human reality). They are made of red rather than yellow hyacinth because, although they belong to the world of Light, their function operates at the lower level of the human figure. Its colour, green, lies between red and black. All this, of course, is an interpretation of the symbolism of colours, not a theory of optics. The entire iconographic symbolism contemplated and meditated upon in the Imam's “celestial” person culminates in the symbolism of the ring.

The ring. The seal worn by the Imam on his finger is made of white hyacinth. In the Imam's case, the seal is the trace of the Lâhût's authority over the Malakût: it is what authenticates his power. Since the light of the Lâhût is white, the Imam's seal is made of white hyacinth.

Finally, the tale tells us that the light of the Imam's Face almost blinded his companions. Qâzî Sa'îd's commentary closes here with a doxology, flowing without any break in tone into the next paragraph (§ 9), which repeats verbatim certain expressions from the celebrated “Sermon of the Theophany” (Khotbat al-bayân).

To understand what is at stake—the Imam as theophany, a manifestation of God—we must return to Qâzî Sa'îd's commentary on the theme of the Face, as it appears in Ibn Bâbûyeh's “Book of Tawhîd.” There the Imam is simultaneously the Face God turns toward humanity (Deus revelatus, God as revealed) and the face humanity turns toward God, since that face is the very form of human religious feeling and faith.

“As for the fact,” Qâzî Sa'îd writes, “that the light of the Imam's Face almost blinded the eyes of his companions, it is because the Imam is the Face of God (Wajh Allah, the theophany), because he is turned wholly toward God, and because he wears no covering made of the Elements that might prevent his being seen at the level of pure light. Blessed, then, are those companions, for they saw with their own eyes—their malakûtî eyes—the Imam in his state of pure light (nûrânîya).

“Even to know the Imams in their state of pure light would be enough to ennoble a soul; how much more so to see them truly. According to one hadith, whoever does not know the Imams in their state of pure light does not know them with the knowledge their true being deserves.” These words lead directly into Salmân the Pure's narrative: “At that moment al-Hasan [the Imam's young son] said to him: ‘Father! Solomon son of David was obeyed because he possessed the Seal.

“But by what means is the Commander of the Faithful [that is, you yourself] obeyed?’ The Imam answered: ‘My child! I am the Face of God, the Eye of God, the Tongue of God. I am the Friend of God. I am the Light of God. I am God's Treasure upon the Earth. I am power, and I am the manifestation of that power. I am paradise, and I am hell’” (§ 9).

The Imam's answer takes up themes found in the “Sermon of the Theophany” and certain hadiths. Historical criticism loses its authority over such sermons and traditions, because even if we dispute their attribution to the First Imam, 'Alî ibn Abî Tâlib, they nonetheless give voice to the eternal Imam as Shiite gnosis understands him: the primordial theophanic Reality without which the Hidden One (Absconditum) would remain forever the unknown and unknowable God.

We should particularly notice the change of clothing that precedes and announces this transfiguration, for it is a familiar symbol in the rituals of the mystery religions. To take off one garment and put on another is the quintessential act of passing from one world to another.
